  "text": "In the spring she had the kitchen window mended.

It was a small thing. The putty had fallen out along the bottom edge, and for two winters she had kept a folded cloth there against the draught. The glazier came on a Tuesday. He drank his tea standing and left white thumbprints on the latch.

Afterward the room was strangely quiet.

Maren washed the cloth and hung it outside. She had forgotten its blue stripe.

There were other things. A bill paid. The heel of a boot repaired. One afternoon she bought pears, though they were dear and had come a long way. She ate one over the sink. Juice ran to her wrist.

At night she went up.

Erris no longer waited every evening. There were friends now, and a bicycle with a loose mudguard. Sometimes Maren heard it rattling along the harbour road before she saw the girl.

Once they passed without speaking. Erris lifted a hand from the handlebars. Maren lifted hers.

She was glad of that afterward.

In June, looking for string, she found a packet of her mother's seeds beneath the kitchen drawer. Lettuce. The paper had softened at the corners. Agnes had written the year on it, and nothing else.

Maren planted them in a shallow box by the mended window.

Most did not come up.

Three did, pale loops lifting grains of earth. She turned the box each morning so they would grow straight.

Before leaving for the lighthouse, she touched the soil with one bare finger. If it was dry, she watered it."

  "text": "By August the lettuce had gone bitter. Maren ate it anyway, with bread and a little salt, leaving one plant to grow tall beside the window.

Erris came on the last Thursday before school. She had fixed the mudguard herself. There was grease beneath her nails, and she wanted to borrow a ruler.

Maren found one in the drawer where the seeds had been.

‘Keep it,’ she said.

That evening, at the lighthouse, the clock stopped while she was writing. She noticed the silence before she noticed the hands.

For a moment she stayed quite still. Below the open window, water moved among the stones with the sound of someone handling paper.

Then she fetched the key.

The mechanism resisted, caught, began again. She checked her watch and set the hands four minutes forward. In the log she wrote: Clock stopped. Wound and reset.

There was room beneath for more. She put the pen away.

On her way down she found a small feather on the stair. No windows were open on that side. She carried it outside, where it clung to her sleeve until she brushed it loose.

The village windows were lit. Someone was frying onions; someone called a dog twice by the same name.

At home the tall lettuce leaned against the glass. Maren moved its box a little farther back and stood looking at the narrow leaves.

She would need an envelope when the seed was ready. There were several in the drawer, saved from bills, which she could turn inside out."

  "text": "The seed came loose in September, smaller than Maren had expected. She shook it onto a saucer and folded an envelope around it. Inside, where no one would see unless they opened the seams, was the amount she had owed for electricity in March.

She wrote Lettuce on the clean side. Then the year.

At the harbour, the boats were being lifted out. Their undersides emerged green and furred, each carrying a waterline that looked permanent until someone began to scrub.

Erris brought back the ruler.

‘You said keep it, but we have three.’

Maren took it. One edge had a notch she did not remember.

They walked to the lighthouse together. On the stairs Erris counted aloud, then stopped before the landing.

‘Did I miss one?’

‘Probably,’ Maren said.

She unlocked the clock case. Erris watched her wind it and asked to try. Maren guided the girl's hand until she felt the resistance.

‘There. No farther.’

The ticking continued, loud in the open case. Maren shut the glass.

That night she entered the tides for the coming week. Beside Thursday she found a faint pencil mark, almost a figure, almost nothing. She rubbed it with her thumb, which made it less legible without removing it.

At home she put the seed envelope in the drawer with the ruler. Some of the seed had escaped onto the table. She gathered it with a damp fingertip, carefully, although there was already more than she could use.

Outside, a boat knocked against the quay. After a while, someone went down to tighten its rope."
